text: Welcome to your consultation. I see you are presenting with a painful, ulcerative skin lesion on your leg. To understand the cause, can you tell me how long the lesion has been present and what it looked like when it first appeared?

speaker: Patient
text: 54-year-old woman. The patient reports a skin lesion on her right leg that has been present for 1 month. The lesion began as a small red spot and has increased in size. She recalls an ant bite at the site before the lesion developed. She has a history of anterior uveitis treated with corticosteroids 8 months ago, as well as Crohn's disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypertension.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Pyoderma Gangrenosum.

The clinical picture of a rapidly enlarging, painful ulcer with a central necrotic base and purplish irregular borders, preceded by trauma (ant bite) in a patient with Crohn's disease and diabetes, is highly suggestive of Pyoderma Gangrenosum. The presence of pitting edema and tortuous veins raises concern for underlying chronic venous insufficiency or deep vein thrombosis, which could be contributing factors or mimics. I will order a wound culture and MRI of the leg to rule out osteomyelitis and deep venous thrombosis before proceeding with a skin biopsy. REQUEST TEST: Wound_Culture, MRI_Leg.
